summary: This standards-track document defines labels for Generalized MPLS to be used with lambda-switch-capable routers, which switch optical wavelengths. The labels identify specific wavelengths, so equipment from different vendors can agree on which one carries a given connection, including in flexible spacing of channels.

plainLanguage.summary: Fiber carries many colors of light at once. This document gives each color a name that routers understand, so they can agree which color a connection uses.

subtitle: A standard 32-bit label that names a specific optical wavelength so lambda-switching equipment from different vendors can agree.

tldr.problem: GMPLS wavelength labels only have meaning between two neighbors, so networks built from different vendors' lambda-switching equipment have no common way to name a wavelength.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a 32-bit label with a Grid, a channel spacing, an Identifier and a signed integer n. The ITU-T DWDM or CWDM grid, the spacing and n together give a frequency or wavelength.
tldr.outcome: Domains can signal the same wavelength in GMPLS signaling and routing protocols, and the RFC adds three IANA subregistries for the Grid and channel spacing codes.

today: RFC 6205 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3471. It has itself been updated by RFC 7699 and RFC 8359.

sections.title: Why Wavelengths Need Standard Labels
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends MPLS beyond packet switching to four more classes of interface: Layer-2 Switch Capable, Time-Division Multiplex Capable, Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) and Fiber Switch Capable. This RFC deals with LSC equipment, such as Reconfigurable Optical Add/Drop Multiplex (ROADM) and Wavelength Cross-Connect (WXC) devices, which switch at the level of a single wavelength.

RFC 3471 says that wavelength label values only have significance between two neighbors, and global wavelength semantics are not considered. To help equipment interoperate, this RFC defines a standard lambda label format compliant with the ITU-T Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) grid, G.694.1, and the Coarse Wavelength Division Multiplexing (CWDM) grid, G.694.2. It updates RFC 3471.
sections.plainLanguage: Light in a fiber comes in many colors. This RFC gives each color a name that everyone agrees on, instead of each neighbor using its own private nickname.

sections.title: The Multi-Vendor Network Problem
sections.content:
The RFC pictures an all-optical network made of different vendors' domains. Vendor A's domain has ROADMs or WXCs, and Vendor B's has Photonic Cross-Connects (PXCs) with DWDM multiplexers and demultiplexers.

Consider a bidirectional label switched path (LSP) from Node-1 to Node-9 set up with GMPLS RSVP-TE. To meet the wavelength continuity constraint, one fixed wavelength (lambda 1) has to be used in both domains. The Path message carries an Upstream_Label object and a Label_Set object holding the same value, and each node switches on that wavelength label. If a node has a tunable transponder, the tuning counts as part of the switching operation.

Without a standard label, each manufacturer may use its own representation, which burdens operators with enforcing policy and invites misconfiguration through manual provisioning. So the RFC says the ITU-T grids should be followed for wavelength labels. How the path is calculated (CSPF) is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If two toy makers each name colors differently, you cannot order a red block across both. One shared color chart avoids the mix-up.

sections.title: How Grid, Spacing and n Give a Wavelength
sections.content:
The label has to identify the table (grid), the channel spacing and a value n from which the frequency or wavelength can be calculated. No new label type is needed, because the field holds either a port label or a wavelength label; only the wavelength label is defined here.

For DWDM, the ITU-T grid is based on nominal central frequencies:

Frequency (THz) = 193.1 THz + n * channel spacing (THz)

Here n is a two's-complement integer (positive, negative or zero) and the channel spacing is 0.0125, 0.025, 0.05 or 0.1 THz. A wider spacing such as 0.2 THz can be reached by combining a narrower spacing with a suitable n. The channel spacing is used only to specify a frequency in signaling, not to show what an LSR is capable of.

For CWDM the channels are 20 nm apart, and:

Wavelength (nm) = 1471 nm + n * 20 nm

Again n is a two's-complement integer. The RFC does not use a channel index, because the grids are not numbered and change as spacing changes with technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick a starting color, a step size, and say how many steps away you want. That one number tells everyone exactly which color you mean.

sections.title: The Wavelength Label Format
sections.content:
Both the DWDM and CWDM labels use the same 32-bit layout of four fields. Grid (3 bits) is 1 for the ITU-T DWDM grid and 2 for the ITU-T CWDM grid; 0 is reserved and 3 to 7 are for future use.

C.S., the channel spacing (4 bits), is for DWDM 1 for 100 GHz, 2 for 50, 3 for 25 and 4 for 12.5, with 0 reserved and 5 to 15 for future use. For CWDM, 1 means 20 nm, 0 is reserved and 2 to 15 are for future use.

The Identifier (9 bits) tells apart different lasers in one node that can transmit the same frequency. It is assigned and scoped per node and MAY change on a per-hop basis. A node MAY pick any value, including zero, but once chosen it MUST NOT change until the LSP is torn down, and it MUST be used in all LSP-related messages such as Resv messages and label RRO subobjects. The one special case is a label ERO subobject: there zero lets the referenced node assign any Identifier, while a non-zero value MUST be used by that node.

The last field is n (16 bits), a two's-complement integer used in the formula above.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is a short note with four boxes: which color chart, how big the steps are, which of several identical lamps, and how many steps from the starting color.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the DWDM example, Node 1 signals an LSP to Node 9 using the DWDM grid, 50 GHz spacing and a wavelength of 193.35 THz. Grid is 1, C.S. is 2, and n comes from (193.35 - 193.1) / 0.05, which is 5.

In the CWDM example, Node 4 signals an LSP to Node 7 using a 20 nm spacing and a wavelength of 1331 nm. Grid is 2, C.S. is 1, and n is (1331 - 1471) / 20, which is -7.
sections.plainLanguage: To name a color, you count how many steps it is from the starting color, forward or backward. Five steps up in one example, seven steps down in the other.

sections.title: IANA Subregistries
sections.content:
IANA has added three subregistries to the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry: Grid, DWDM Channel Spacing and CWDM Channel Spacing. Their initial entries match the value tables above, with the unassigned ranges left open.

New values in each subregistry are assigned by Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of which numbers mean which color chart or step size, and adding to it takes a formal approval.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations beyond RFC 3471 and RFC 3473. For a general discussion of MPLS and GMPLS security it points to the framework in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming the colors does not add any new ways for trouble to sneak in, so the older safety rules still apply.

fields.name: Grid
fields.desc: 1 for ITU-T DWDM, 2 for ITU-T CWDM.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Per-node value that tells lasers apart.

fields.name: n
fields.desc: Two's-complement integer used to compute the frequency or wavelength.
